entries.title: Former White Sox player Andruw Jones inducted into Baseball Hall of Fame
entries.summary: <p>COOPERSTOWN, N.Y. — Andruw Jones will be most remembered for his 12 seasons as a stunning center fielder and 10-time Gold Glove winner with the Braves. But he thinks fondly about playing the 2010 season with the White Sox near the end of his career.</p><p>‘‘I love Chicago,’’ Jones said during a media session Saturday at the Clark Sports Center.</p><p>How much does he love Chicago?</p><p>‘‘Two years ago, I wanted to go to the Chicago Cubs and watch a game [at Wrigley Field] against the Braves,’’ he said. ‘‘I sat in the center-field bleachers. I loved it because I saw so much joy that those people were having. So I do love Chicago.’’</p><p>Jones was inducted Sunday into the National Baseball Hall of Fame, along with fellow outfielder Carlos Beltran and second baseman Jeff Kent.</p><p>Jones made it on his ninth of a maximum 10 tries, earning 78.4% of the votes from the 425 ballots cast by eligible members of the Baseball Writers’ Association of America. It was worth the wait.</p><p>Opening his speech in front of a record 57 returning Hall of Famers, Jones said: ‘‘Wow, this is an amazing feeling. First of all, I want to thank baseball writers for voting me into the Hall. Getting that phone call was the most memorable moment in my life. There’s no greater honor in baseball than to be here.’’</p><p>Jones thanked his late ballplaying father, Henry; his late Braves manager and fellow Hall of Famer, Bobby Cox; the late Hank Aaron; and former Braves teammate and Hall of Famer Chipper Jones, who never let him waver and always promoted his candidacy.</p><p>‘‘The Jones boys are in Cooperstown now,’’ Andruw said.</p><p>Jones speaks five languages and is the first native of Curacao to make the Hall. He addressed his countrymen for a moment in their own language, Papiamentu, saying how proud he is to be from that country.</p><p>Jones played 17 seasons with five teams, but he was best known for coming up as a 19-year-old with the Braves as a fleet-footed center fielder. His defense made life easier for now-Hall of Fame brothers and former Braves pitchers Greg Maddux, Tom Glavine and John Smoltz. He highlighted that first season with a pair of home runs in Game 1 of the 1996 World Series at Yankee Stadium, but the Braves ultimately lost that series to the Yankees.</p><p>Jones recalled that he never wanted to leave the Braves, but he did so after the 2007 season, signing with the Dodgers as a free agent for two years at $36.2 million.</p><p>‘‘The Braves were the first team that gave me the opportunity to fall in love and chase a dream,’’ Jones said Saturday. ‘‘I really didn’t want to leave because it was tough to leave an organization that gave me that chance. You fall in love with the city, you marry and your kids grow up there and your home is there. So it was tough leaving.’’</p><p>His single season with the Dodgers was a disaster. He was overweight, suffered torn cartilage in his right knee and batted .158 in only 75 games. The Dodgers cut their losses after that season and paid him $21.4 million to play elsewhere.</p><p>‘‘I didn’t play the way I wanted to play,’’ Jones said about his year in Los Angeles.</p><p>Jones then bounced from the Rangers to the White Sox, who paid him the minimum of $500,000 in 2010, before finishing his big-league career with the Yankees.</p><p>He played in 107 games for the Sox, batting .230 with 19 homers, 48 RBI and an .827 OPS. Not too shabby.</p><p>‘‘I went to Chicago, and [then-manager] Ozzie Guillen told me, ‘Hey, if you come in in shape, I’m gonna play you,’ ’’ Jones said. ‘‘So I worked hard, I got ready and I had a great year. I carried the team for a little while during the first half. But Chicago was fun. I had a great time. Enjoyed<br>everybody, every bit of it.</p><p>‘‘I played in some great cities: Atlanta, Los Angeles, Chicago and finishing in New York. Even Japan was awesome, where I played two years and won a championship. I mean, I was very lucky.’’<br></p>

entries.title: A new Illinois law keeps hospital finances hidden from the public
entries.summary: <p>A new law in Illinois requires hospitals to file more financial information with state regulators, giving them a deeper look into whether medical centers are struggling.</p><p>But these records will be hidden from the public, <a class="Link" href="https://ilga.gov/Legislation/PublicActs/PrinterFriendly/104-0470" target="_blank" ><u>the law states</u></a>, limiting how much patients, their doctors and even community leaders like city councils know about hospitals in their back yards.</p><p>This is one piece of a broad law Gov. JB Pritzker signed in June “to support at-risk hospitals, strengthen our statewide care infrastructure, and defend the interests of patients and taxpayers,” he said in a news release at the time.</p><p>The law also creates a new loan program for distressed hospitals and requires hospitals <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/health-medicine/2026/07/11/where-do-they-go-what-west-side-patients-face-after-another-hospital-closes-west-suburban-medical-center" target="_blank" ><u>in debt to the state</u></a> to submit wind-down plans in case they close.</p><p>State lawmakers approved the new law unanimously, records show. It’s more than 500 pages. But after WBEZ raised questions about shielding hospital finances from the public, some now say they either don’t support that part of the law or suggest it could be changed.</p><p>“I don't support the fact that this is not available for the public to see,” said West Side state Rep. La Shawn Ford. “I think that the community deserves to know” whether a hospital is healthy or not.</p><p>A for-profit hospital on the edge of his district, West Suburban Medical Center in Oak Park, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/health-medicine/2026/04/01/west-suburban-medical-center-struggled-treat-patients-closed-vows-to-reopen-weiss-memorial-inspection-reports-oak-park" target="_blank" ><u>abruptly closed</u></a> in March. Its owner closed the hospital <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/health-medicine/2025/08/08/weiss-memorial-hospital-emergency-room-in-uptown-closes" target="_blank" ><u>and Weiss Memorial</u></a> in Uptown last year, owing the state more than $100 million in advances, taxes and penalties. The state has recouped at least $13 million so far.</p><p>Located across the street from Austin, West Suburban was a destination for the majority Black neighborhood, which has <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/health-medicine/chicagos-death-gap" target="_blank" ><u>one of the lowest life expectancies</u></a> in Chicago.</p><p>Now a quick trip in an emergency has turned into a 10- to 20-minute drive to hospitals already stretched thin or have emergency departments so packed they’re on the cusp of turning away ambulances, a recent <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/health-medicine/2026/07/11/where-do-they-go-what-west-side-patients-face-after-another-hospital-closes-west-suburban-medical-center" target="_blank" ><u>WBEZ/Sun-Times investigation</u></a> found.</p><p>Doctors fear more hospitals could close next year when <a class="Link" href="https://cookcountyhealth.org/press-release/get-medicaid-facts-new-site-and-toolkit-launched-to-educate-public-about-looming-medicaid-eligibility-changes/" target="_blank" ><u>big cuts to Medicaid</u></a> public health insurance for people who are poor or have disabilities take effect. More than 400,000 people <a class="Link" href="https://www.rwjf.org/en/insights/our-research/2026/03/millions-could-lose-health-coverage-due-to-new-rules.html" target="_blank" ><u>could lose coverage</u></a>, meaning less money for hospitals that treat them.</p><p>In the new law, hospitals licensed by the state must file audited financial statements, as well as balance sheets detailing their assets, liabilities and net worth. Audited statements are considered the <a class="Link" href="https://www.kff.org/health-costs/gaps-in-data-about-hospital-and-health-system-finances-limit-transparency-for-policymakers-and-patients/" target="_blank" ><u>gold standard for hospital financial reporting</u></a>, said Zachary Levinson, who leads the Project on Hospital Costs at KFF, a non-partisan health policy organization.</p><p>These details offer a window into where a hospital’s money comes from, and how much they’re making versus losing. They show whether a hospital can invest in their facilities to improve the quality of care for patients, or if they need more resources to prevent closing or reducing services.</p><p>As Medicaid cuts looms, a hospital’s finances could offer an advanced warning — in particular for people who rely on their local hospital, Levinson said.</p><p>“I can understand why a health system might not want to disclose some information to the public,” Levinson said. “But I can’t really think of what the benefit to the public is of keeping this data under wraps.”</p><p>Under the new law, Illinois hospitals’ financial information would not be subject to the state’s open records laws or even a subpoena. The state could release aggregated information, or a summary, that would not name specific hospitals, the law states.</p><p>Pritzker, a billionaire businessman and an heir to the Hyatt hotel fortune, declined an interview. In a statement, he said: “Ultimately, hospitals are private entities, and the inclusion of a privacy clause in the new law reflects the understanding that detailed, private financial data must be handled in a sensitive manner."</p><p>In Illinois, hospitals already provide some financial information to the state that’s accessible to the public. For example, a <a class="Link" href="https://hfsrb.illinois.gov/content/dam/soi/en/web/hfsrb/documents/inventories-data/hospital/facility-profiles/2024/2024-Hospital-Profiles-Individual.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>hospital profile</u></a>, of sorts, spells out how much revenue they make each year, number of patients they treat and services they provide.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://www.kff.org/state-health-policy-data/state-indicator/hospitals-by-ownership/?currentTimeframe=0&sortModel=%7B%22colId%22:%22Location%22,%22sort%22:%22asc%22%7D" target="_blank" ><u>majority of hospitals </u></a>in Illinois are nonprofits, according to KFF. Their finances are typically easier to find than a for-profit, from <a class="Link" href="https://www.guidestar.org/" target="_blank" ><u>public tax returns</u></a> filed with the government, to posting their financial statements on their web sites.</p><p>Publicly traded for-profit hospitals must disclose their finances in filings with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. But many others don’t have to.</p><p>State Rep. Anna Moeller, a lead sponsor of the new law, said the new financial reporting requirements create more accountability for hospitals, which are largely funded by the government.</p><p>“There will be more transparency to the state,” said Moeller, an Elgin Democrat. “To the public? No. … But it's something that I think probably merits more discussion.”</p><p>She also leads a bipartisan group of lawmakers overseeing Medicaid issues whose meetings are held behind closed doors. Medicaid is a significant part of the <a class="Link" href="https://budget.illinois.gov/content/dam/soi/en/web/budget/documents/budget-book/fy2027-budget/Fiscal-Year-2027-Operating-Budget.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>state budget</u></a>. Proposed laws debated during the group’s private discussions come up in public hearings, Moeller said.</p><p>Senate President Don Harmon called the new law “a first step.” </p><p>“If we need to fix the law, we know the guys that do that,” said Harmon, a Democrat in Oak Park, where West Suburban closed.</p><p>The Illinois Health and Hospital Association, a powerful lobbyist for hospitals across the state, declined an interview. In a statement, a spokesperson said the state wanted to bring together information that hospitals now report in pieces to analyze the overall condition of the industry.</p><p>The hospital association requested a “confidentiality provision” to protect hospital data that, when viewed in isolation, may not accurately reflect a hospital’s overall financial condition, could be misinterpreted or may contain proprietary business information, the spokesperson said.</p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Jeanne phillips bids adieu as 'dear abby' endures
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR READERS:</b> As anyone who reads "Dear Abby" knows, I have always stressed the importance of writing thank-you notes. It is now time for me to put pen to paper. I have always considered you, my readers, to be my friends. Thank you for accepting me as warmly as you always have and thank you for being willing to share your joys, pains and frustrations with me these many years. Your trust is the greatest honor I have ever been given. You have taught me far more life lessons than I have ever taught you.</p><p>I am now in my 39th year of penning the "Dear Abby" column, which started on Jan. 9, 1956, written by my late mother, Pauline Phillips. When I began writing it in 1987, I promised myself that when the time came to retire, I would step aside to live life without a deadline. I am grateful for the support of my two loyal and able assistants, Steven Andrews and Jose Fuentes. Please don't worry about me; my health is fine. I plan to indulge my long-postponed itch to travel.</p><p>In the years ahead, my column will continue to serve you. It will be written by a capable editorial staff. Please wish me a happy retirement as I open this new chapter of my life.</p><p>I love you all. — Jeanne Phillips aka Dear Abby</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My husband's brother, "Hank," has estranged himself from the family. He's married with two children but has little to no contact with his mom, dad, stepdad, sister, brother (my husband) or any of his nieces and nephews — except when he calls his parents asking for money.</p><p>On the rare occasions I have seen him, his wife refuses to participate in any family gatherings, dinners or even photos. There's always a string of excuses or obvious lies, and none of us can understand why they have chosen to stay so distant. It's painful and confusing.</p><p>Since becoming part of this family, I have watched Hank manipulate situations to get what he wants. He is extremely persuasive and plays the victim well. He is caught in a cycle of being unable to keep a job while trying to maintain a lifestyle far beyond his means.</p><p>I do have some sympathy, because it's clear there are deeper issues behind his behavior, but the pattern of drifting in and out of our lives — especially my in-laws' — has become exhausting. They've finally reached the point where they're no longer willing to give him money, but I worry about the future.</p><p>As my in-laws continue to age and potentially become more vulnerable, I fear Hank will find new ways to take advantage of them. I love them, and it has been painful watching them be used and hurt for so many years. Is there anything I can do? — <i>CONFLICTED IN MISSOURI</i></p><p><b>DEAR CONFLICTED:</b> Manipulating older folks to get them to fork over money is called elder abuse, and there are laws against it. Although it may be a bit premature (as your in-laws are still mentally competent), it couldn't hurt for you and your husband to consult an attorney who specializes in elder law and discuss your concerns, because crimes like this happen too often.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren, also known as Jeanne Phillips, and was founded by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 69440, Los Angeles, CA 90069.</i></p><p>For everything you need to know about wedding planning, order "How to Have a Lovely Wedding." Send your name and mailing address, plus check or money order for $8 (U.S. funds) to: Dear Abby, Wedding Booklet, P.O. Box 446, Kings Mills, OH 45034-0446. (Shipping and handling are included in the price.)</p>

entries.title: Breakthrough pancreatic cancer drug illustrates importance of research
entries.summary: <p>For families facing pancreatic cancer, every breakthrough represents something deeply personal: more time, more hope and a reason to believe progress is possible.</p><p>Pancreatic cancer does not discriminate by age, race, ethnicity or gender. It has taken the lives of people as young as 30 in perfect health. It could happen to any one of us.</p><p>That is why the results presented at this year's American Society of Clinical Oncology's Annual Meeting are so encouraging. Researchers reported in Phase 3 clinical data, the new drug <a class="Link" href="https://ascopost.com/issues/june-10-2026/daraxonrasib-nearly-doubles-survival-in-previously-treated-metastatic-pancreatic-cancer/" target="_blank" >daraxonrasib nearly doubled</a> survival and reduced the risk of death by 60% for patients with previously treated metastatic pancreatic cancer, which is a remarkable advance against one of the deadliest cancers.</p><p>At the <a class="Link" href="https://www.rolfefoundation.org/" target="_blank" >Rolfe Pancreatic Cancer Foundation</a>, we know breakthroughs like this do not happen overnight. They are built on years of investment in innovative science, collaboration among researchers and the willingness to fund bold ideas before success is certain. That belief is at the heart of our mission to support groundbreaking research, particularly in early detection, while providing patients and families with the resources and hope they need throughout their journey.</p><p>This progress should also serve as a reminder to policymakers. Medical innovation depends on an environment that encourages sustained research and development. Policies that weaken incentives to invest in biomedical research ultimately put future breakthroughs and future patients at risk.</p><p>For the more than 67,000 Americans diagnosed with pancreatic cancer each year, scientific progress cannot come soon enough. Every new therapy builds on decades of research and brings us one step closer to a future where pancreatic cancer is detected earlier, treated more effectively and, ultimately, no longer a devastating diagnosis.</p><p>Pancreatic cancer is personal to us, which is why we believe every scientific breakthrough matters. We are committed to advancing research and supporting patients and families because today's discoveries create tomorrow's hope for earlier detection, more effective treatments and better outcomes.</p><p><i>Stacia Hart, executive director, Rolfe Pancreatic Cancer Foundation</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-db0000" name="module-db0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Ammons’ indictment exposes electoral flaws</h3><p>As a University of Illinois student, I voted for state Rep. Carol Ammons, D-Urbana, twice while living in Champaign-Urbana. She built her reputation as an advocate for students, higher education and the local community. That's what makes the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/07/10/carol-ammons-indictment-illinois-house-harry-benton-resign" >allegations</a> against her so disappointing.</p><p>Federal prosecutors allege Ammons directed state grant funding to nonprofits that employed her daughter despite being warned it created an impermissible conflict of interest. They also allege Ammons and her husband, Champaign County Clerk Aaron Ammons, later sought to obstruct the federal investigation.</p><p>Public office depends on trust. Once that trust is broken, it's incredibly difficult to restore.</p><p>If the allegations are true, funding that should have benefited the Champaign-Urbana community instead became a vehicle to benefit one political family. Students and taxpayers deserved better from someone who campaigned on serving them.</p><p>Carol Ammons' indictment also exposes a larger problem. Illinois still relies too heavily on the honor system when it comes to ethics, and accountability at the ballot box has also been lacking. Since taking office in 2014 as a state representative, Ammons has faced just three challengers, including primary elections. She has never received less than 60% of the vote in a general election and has run unopposed in most of her races.</p><p>When elections aren't competitive, voters have fewer opportunities to hold elected officials accountable before problems escalate. Illinois needs stronger conflict-of-interest laws, an independent legislative watchdog and an independent redistricting commission that gives voters meaningful choices instead of protecting incumbents.</p><p>The state’s voters deserve representatives who earn their trust and a system that holds them accountable when they don't.</p><p><i>Micky Horstman, communications manager, Illinois Policy</i></p><h3>Men’s behavior — not women’s — must change to stop rapes</h3><p>There was one item in Robert Herguth’s recent Sun-Times <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/07/15/country-thunder-music-festival-twin-lakes-wisconsin-chicago-area-sexual-assaults" >story</a> about the sexual assaults associated with the Country Thunder music festival that was the most terrifying: Kenosha County’s board of supervisors chairman Mark Nordigian encouraging female concertgoers to engage in a “buddy system” to protect themselves during the event in his community.</p><p>Female concertgoers are not the ones who need to change their behavior. How about suggesting a buddy system for male concertgoers to, you know, stop raping?</p><p><i>Don Anderson, Oak Park</i></p><h3>Paying attention</h3><p>I spent my younger years living with the possibility of being drafted. I wonder if today's young men know <a class="Link" href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/04/09/politics/us-military-draft-registration-2026" target="_blank" >automatic military draft registration</a> will be starting in December.</p><p>Men between 18 to 26 are already supposed to register for selective service in case a draft is required.</p><p>But soon, the responsibility for registering <a class="Link" href="https://time.com/article/2026/04/09/us-men-automatic-military-draft-change/" target="_blank" >“will shift from individual men to SSS through integration with federal data sources</a>," according to the Selective Service System.</p><p>Hey guys, you better get off those useless apps and get involved in our political process before you find yourself marching off to fight some mindless war.</p><p><i>Warren Rodgers Jr., Orland Park</i></p><h3>U.S. military deaths</h3><p>'Mr.' President, how many U.S. service members <a class="Link" href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/jul/21/us-military-third-service-member-jordan-attack" target="_blank" >must die</a> before you determine your criminal war on Iran has failed and must be ended on Iran's sensible terms?'</p><p><i>Walt Zlotow, Glen Ellyn</i></p><h3>Unintentional comedy</h3><p>White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt deserves plaudits and should consider a career in comedy for <a class="Link" href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/watch-trump-believes-his-kalshi-betting-teleprompter-operator-is-a-disgrace-leavitt-says" target="_blank" >delivering</a> the funniest one-liner of the year: "There are very strict ethical guidelines here at the White House."</p><p><i>Larry Niemi, Loop</i></p><h3>Big daddy</h3><p>Vice President JD Vance says because of the importance of his job, he won't take <a class="Link" href="https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/jd-vance-refuses-paternity-leave-074502232.html" target="_blank" >paternity leave</a><b> </b>after the birth of his fourth child.</p><p>Maybe the prospect of changing diapers was also a factor. Then again, the Vances can afford to hire an au pair. Or two.</p><p><i>Dan McGuire, Bensenville</i></p>

entries.title: 'Act of God' an excuse for government's poor flood preparation
entries.summary: <p>This summer, severe storms and extreme heat have crippled infrastructure across major cities.</p><p>I was on a call with a friend in Chicago when she mentioned her basement had flooded.</p><p>"You might hear some banging," she said as repair crews worked through the damage.</p><p>When I asked about flood insurance, she said she had none.</p><p>Floods are historically labeled an "<a class="Link" href="https://www.investopedia.com/terms/a/act-god.asp" target="_blank" >act of God</a>," requiring special insurance coverage. But Chicago isn't a bayou or a vulnerable coastal town. It is a lakefront architectural ambition with phenomenal infrastructure. Blaming God feels like a stretch.</p><p>The sump pump, a recent discovery in my home, is a long-standing necessity for Chicago residents. Basements frequently flood, not because of acts of God but because of historically poor drainage and legacy sewage systems.</p><p>Flooding is the most <a class="Link" href="https://www.fema.gov/pdf/media/factsheets/2010/flooding_what_know_fs.pdf" target="_blank" >frequent and costly natural disaster</a> in the U.S., according to the Federal Emergency Management Agency. It has affected <a class="Link" href="https://www.floodsmart.gov/get-flood-insurance" target="_blank" >99% of U.S. counties</a> over the last three decades. <a class="Link" href="https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/billions/" target="_blank" ></a><a class="Link" href="https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/billions/" target="_blank" ></a> <a class="Link" href="https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/articles/99-u-counties-flooded-over-110000399.html?guccounter=1&guce_referrer=aHR0cHM6Ly93d3cuZ29vZ2xlLmNvbS8&guce_referrer_sig=AQAAAAOMHUdmIAcOF_gajdetzOORXwWRPYvNGLQ8CB7rr104SGuAMb8q92BRZQP621q4fvaXditm8JG5Qn-Td_iMDkrJDZ61MTevhiCGIXgZb5LLdfyi98ORHk2VJWCVPg9jzGk-5CFSugOcCp2dTKlnzagDuchP9WQDJnAHYDccloUX" target="_blank" ></a> Yet only about <a class="Link" href="https://www.floodsmart.gov/get-flood-insurance" target="_blank" >4%</a> of U.S. homeowners carry flood insurance, according to FEMA. Standard homeowners’ policies explicitly exclude it, <a class="Link" href="https://www.allstate.com/resources/home-insurance/water-damage" target="_blank" >no matter the cause</a>.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-280000" name="module-280000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>While at least one climate risk model classifies Chicago as having a "<a class="Link" href="https://firststreet.org/city/chicago-il/1714000_fsid/flood" target="_blank" >minor overall risk</a>" of flooding, the human toll on the ground tells a vastly different story.</p><p>About 484,800 adults across the city experienced residential flooding in 2024 alone, according to the <a class="Link" href="https://chicagohealthatlas.org/" target="_blank" >Chicago Health Atlas</a>, a website created by the Chicago Department of Public Health and the Population Health Analytics Metrics Evaluation, or PHAME, Center at University of Illinois Chicago, which shares data with the public on health-related issues. With 41,200 affected residents, the West Side community of Austin bears the city's heaviest burden, according to the data, exposing severe localized vulnerabilities.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-510000" name="image-510000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/e14977a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1052x590+0+82/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb8%2F2f%2Fee955b3547809c38a29125be7da5%2Fscreenshot-2026-07-24-at-9-21-59-am.png 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/45a4df9/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1052x590+0+82/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb8%2F2f%2Fee955b3547809c38a29125be7da5%2Fscreenshot-2026-07-24-at-9-21-59-am.png 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d23b520/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1052x590+0+82/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb8%2F2f%2Fee955b3547809c38a29125be7da5%2Fscreenshot-2026-07-24-at-9-21-59-am.png" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Inches of water surrounding a bed in a basement. The bed has clothes piled on it. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d23b520/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1052x590+0+82/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb8%2F2f%2Fee955b3547809c38a29125be7da5%2Fscreenshot-2026-07-24-at-9-21-59-am.png 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b6a8f07/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1052x590+0+82/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb8%2F2f%2Fee955b3547809c38a29125be7da5%2Fscreenshot-2026-07-24-at-9-21-59-am.png 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d23b520/2147483647/strip/true/crop/1052x590+0+82/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fb8%2F2f%2Fee955b3547809c38a29125be7da5%2Fscreenshot-2026-07-24-at-9-21-59-am.png" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Destroyed belongings sit in the flooded basement of a home in the Austin neighborhood in 2023. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Provided</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>Failure of human policy</h3><h3></h3><p>But we must ask: At what point does a hazard this predictable and frequent stop being an act of God and instead become a clear failure of human policy?</p><p>If the state knows where the water will go, and the city knows its <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicago.gov/city/en/depts/water/supp_info/basement_floodingpartnership.html" target="_blank" >infrastructure</a> is incapable of containing it, blaming God is inaccurate — though it remains a convenient defense against an otherwise intractable problem.</p><p>As a professor of translational geoAI at the University of Maryland, I use satellite data and artificial intelligence to tackle real-world vulnerabilities, creating policy-ready intelligence for disaster risk management to identify failure points, opportunities for improvement and practical applications. What Chicago is experiencing is not an isolated meteorological event. It is a clear failure of policy to keep pace with a changing climate.</p><p>We often have the data to see these disasters coming, yet we continue to treat predictable infrastructure failures as unavoidable acts of God.</p><p>Chicago has no hurricane season, and its flooding doesn't stem from its riverbanks bursting. Yet it faces one of the most <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2026/07/07/chicago-flooding-stormwater-mayor-brandon-johnson-climate-change-deep-tunnel-west-side" >persistent</a> urban drainage crises in the country — one that remains largely invisible because it happens underground, in basements, in neighborhoods that rarely make the national news.</p><p>The city's combined sewer system, which handles both stormwater and sanitary sewage in a single network, dates to the late 19th century. It was built for a different climate, with steadier rains that fell gradually enough for the system to absorb.</p><p>What Chicago gets now are storms that drop 2 or more inches in a single hour. When the system fills, water reverses, coming up through basement floor drains as a mix of stormwater and raw sewage, into furnaces, water heaters, electrical panels and everything a family has stored below grade.</p><h3>Disastrous flooding in 2023</h3><h3></h3><p>In 2023, an estimated <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/04/14/chicago-flooding-mold-health-climate-weather-rain-planning-soaked" >70,000</a> Chicago-area homes flooded, the Sun-Times reported. Residents in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/01/09/record-breaking-rainfall-leaves-hundreds-of-streets-and-basements-flooded" >71 of the city’s 77 neighborhoods</a> filed flooding complaints in a single storm event in January, according to the Sun-Times.</p><p>The Illinois Department of Natural Resources reports a little more than <a class="Link" href="https://dnr.illinois.gov/content/dam/soi/en/web/dnr/cmp/documents/program/section309/IDNR-CMP%20Assessment%20and%20Strategy%202026%20to%202030%20DRAFT.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com" target="_blank" >42%</a> of Cook County is now covered in impervious surface: roads, parking lots and driveways that shed water rather than absorb it, concentrating every rainstorm into a surge the sewers cannot swallow.</p><p>The communities absorbing the worst of it are on the South and West sides — older, disinvested neighborhoods of color with legacy infrastructure and fewer resources for retrofitting, yet they accounted for <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagofed.org/publications/blogs/chicago-fed-insights/2020/chicago-flood-risk" target="_blank" >72%</a> of the city's flood damage claims in 2020, the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago reported. The communities also remain entirely excluded from FEMA risk maps.</p><p>In 2023, the Sun-Times <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2026/05/17/chicago-basement-flooding-insurance-state-farm-fema-cook-county-soaked" >reported</a> a resident had $70,000 in damage after 5 feet of sewage shot through a floor drain. Insurance covered nothing in a county where fewer than 1% of homeowners carry flood coverage.</p><p>Flood insurance is unattainable for many, and expecting homeowners to shoulder tens of thousands of dollars in damage and retrofitting costs is not realistic.</p><p>Floods become disasters only when humans are left in the path of predictable harm. At some point, we have to stop calling it an act of God and call it what it is: a failure of infrastructure and policy not keeping pace with a changing climate.</p><p><i>Catherine Nakalembe is a professor of translational geoAI, bridging geoscience with artificial intelligence to address real-world problems, at the University of Maryland, and a Public Voices Fellow of The OpEd Project.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-170000" name="module-170000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: George Clinton expands his Afrofuturist universe through paintings, now on display in Chicago
entries.summary: <p>As a boundary-pushing pioneer of funk music, George Clinton imagined entire mythologies of beings from outer space.</p><p>He encountered them, too.</p><p>The pivotal moment occurred one morning in 1976, as he and bassist Bootsy Collins drove from Detroit to Clinton’s home in Canada.</p><p>“We saw a laser light, right out of the clouds, hit the ground,” said Clinton, now 85 and living in Florida.</p><p>A few miles away, that same piercing light struck their car, and dripped a mercury-like substance on the hood. Suddenly, it was nighttime, as though they’d sped through hours in mere moments.</p><p>“When we got to my house, my daughter said, ‘Y'all look like you’ve seen a ghost,’” Clinton said.</p><p>That experience is referenced in Clinton’s painting, “In the Daytime, Bobba!,” which depicts a white spaceship hovering over Earth and against an intense blue sky. It is displayed with other works in his art show, “<a class="Link" href="https://marianeibrahim.com/exhibitions/123-george-clinton-mothership/overview/" target="_blank" ><u>Mothership</u></a>,” which opened Saturday at Mariane Ibrahim Gallery in West Town, and remains on view through Sept. 5.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure Town.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Though he is colorblind, he has created a variety of vibrant motherships using acrylic, spray paint and charcoal. The exhibit even includes a tiny replica of the<a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/03/12/arts/music/p-funk-mothership-george-clinton.html" target="_blank" ><u> iconic, $500,000 spaceship</u></a> that he debuted on his P-Funk Earth Tour in 1976. Building upon the universe he created as the leader of Parliament-Funkadelic, his visual art underscores his contribution to <a class="Link" href="https://nmaahc.si.edu/explore/exhibitions/afrofuturism" target="_blank" ><u>Afrofuturism</u></a>, a cultural movement that envisions a future of liberation for Black people.</p><p>“He is a pre-internet architect of Afrofuturism vocabulary and imagery,”<b> </b>said Mariane Ibrahim, a French-Somali gallerist who also owns spaces in Paris and Mexico City. </p><p>“To think about Black bodies in the cosmic [realm], as technological bodies, he was one of the first artists to engage with that. My parents used to look at him like, ‘He’s totally crazy.’ But this craziness had the color of my skin, so I felt entitled to be crazy as well, to free myself.”</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-430000" name="module-430000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><b>“George Clinton: Mothership”</b><br><br><b>When:</b> Through Sept. 5<br><b>Where</b>: 437 N. Paulina St.<br><b>Hours:</b> 11 a.m. - 6 p.m., Tuesday - Saturday<br><b>Info</b>: <a class="Link" href="https://marianeibrahim.com/" target="_blank" >marianeibrahim.com</a></div> </div><p></p><h2>From doodling dogs to displaying at Art Basel</h2><p>Before he started painting, Clinton was a sketch artist, often doodling dogs alongside his autographs. The images became so popular, likely due to his 1982 hit “Atomic Dog,” that people sent him official commissions.</p><p>“Somebody paid me $15,000 to paint a dog,” Clinton said. “And then I sold another one for like $10,000.”</p><p>But it was during the pandemic that Clinton became more focused on visual art, using the downtime to hone his craft. He doesn’t consider his colorblindness to be a hindrance — or his eccentric fashion. While painting, he focuses on shading more than color, though things would get tricky when his kids and grandkids played pranks by switching the labels on his paint jars.</p><p>“I get away with it pretty good because nobody even knew I was colorblind for years,” he said. “Colors don’t clash, I guess, if you don’t know any better.”</p><p>Since securing an art manager and team, Clinton has displayed his art everywhere from Art Basel Miami Beach to the SCAD Museum of Art in Savannah, Georgia. Last year, his paintings of dogs were included in a group exhibition at Mariane Ibrahim’s Paris gallery.</p><p>“These portraits of dogs look so human,” Ibrahim said. “They have personalities. They have attitude. said he didn’t realize graffiti artists were being taken seriously by the art world until recently.</p><p>“Basquiat used to hang around with us,” he said. “We didn’t think of [graffiti] as fine “Mothership,” at Mariane Ibrahim gallery in West Town. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Clinton said he has stayed relevant by changing with the times, whether it was pivoting from the “Motown Sound” to psychedelia or embracing the hip-hop artists who sampled his music. And today, he sees young people enjoying themselves at his shows.</p><p>“We’ve got fans from 12 to 112,” he said. "It’s like going to the circus. Grandparents can go, and parents and kids can go together.”</p><p>That cross-section of people was present at the opening of “Mothership" in Chicago, as people of all ages and races took selfies with Clinton. Older fans brought their kids and grandchildren. Some wore P-Funk T-shirts and brought their records for Clinton to sign. </p><p>Yvette Oduro, 56, of South Shore, said she had “chills” when she saw the music icon.</p><p>“I grew up listening to his records on my mother’s big green stereo that looked like a piece of furniture, perusing through all the album covers, and just imagining what was on the artist’s mind,” she said.</p><p>“He brought such an imagination of what it is to be Black and to transcend anybody else’s ideas of what that is. entries.title: Illinois sees 16% drop in SNAP enrollment one year after food program overhaul
entries.summary: <p>Small hands helped load five boxes of food into the trunk of Irene Salinas Torres’ van.</p><p>“I carried this one,” one child proudly said in Spanish.</p><p>Salinas Torres and her family had stopped by a nonprofit in Pilsen for its monthly food distribution this spring, soon after thousands were expected to lose access to the federal Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program because of expanded work rules and other new restrictions passed by Congress last summer. The mother of five had received $450 in SNAP benefits each month until about March.</p><p>“We limit ourselves from many things,” said Salinas Torres in Spanish. She lost SNAP because her household income had increased once an older son started working. “We just buy the essentials, what you need to eat that day. We don’t get the luxury to buy extra.”</p><p>Over the last year, the SNAP program in Illinois has declined by 16%. By June, the number of SNAP recipients had fallen to nearly 1.6 million, down from nearly 1.9 million last year, according to the Illinois Department of Human Services. That’s the lowest number receiving food assistance in the state since 2009.</p><p>Those who remain are a vulnerable population. Nearly 97% of the people still receiving SNAP were exempted from the expanded work rules because they meet certain requirements, such as living with a physical or mental condition or having a child who is 13 years or younger, according to the state.</p><p>The Illinois Department of Human Services, which administers the program locally, estimates 148,000 people lost SNAP because of the work requirements. State officials had initially estimated <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/01/21/new-snap-work-requirements-cook-county-warn-health-consequences-cut-off-congress-donald-trump-food-stamps" target="_blank" ><u>400,000</u></a> people would lose benefits. Illinois SNAP recipients have fared better than in states that have slashed their programs. Arizona has seen a 50% decrease in SNAP recipients.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-e60000" name="module-e60000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><b>Help for SNAP recipients</b><br><ul class="rte2-style-ul" style="margin-top:0;margin-bottom:0;padding-inline-start:48px;" id="rte-3155f6e0-43f2-11f1-aa5c-b93517248f50"><li><b>Update your SNAP information:</b> Illinois created a <a class="Link" href="https://aberp.illinois.gov/screener/ABAWD?lang=EN" target="_blank" >website</a> where you can check if you meet the new SNAP program requirements. You can update your information by calling 1-800-843-6154. <a class="Link" href="https://aberp.illinois.gov/screener/ABAWD?lang=EN" target="_blank" >https://aberp.illinois.gov/screener/ABAWD?lang=EN</a></li><li><b>Find a food pantry:</b> Here’s a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago/2025/10/29/where-to-find-chicago-area-food-pantries-if-snap-goes-away" target="_blank" >list of pantries</a> in the Chicago area</li><li><b>Where can I volunteer?</b><br><ul class="rte2-style-ul" style="margin-top:0;margin-bottom:0;padding-inline-start:48px;" id="rte-31561df0-43f2-11f1-aa5c-b93517248f50"><li>Meals on Wheels Chicago pantry offers volunteer hours. <a class="Link" href="https://www.mealsonwheelschicago.org/volunteer-individuals-formstack" target="_blank" ><u>Visit</u></a> <a class="Link" href="https://www.mealsonwheelschicago.org/volunteer-individuals-formstack" target="_blank" ><u>https://www.mealsonwheelschicago.org/volunteer-individuals-formstack</u></a></li><li>Volunteer shifts at Nourishing Hope’s pantries are available at <a class="Link" href="https://nourishinghopechi.org/volunteer/" target="_blank" ><u>https://nourishinghopechi.org/volunteer/</u></a></li><li>Care For Friends, 530 W. Fullerton Pkwy., can be reached at (773) 932-1010</li></ul></li></ul></div> </div><p>This month marked one year since President Donald Trump signed into law H.R. 1, a massive tax and spending plan that imposed these changes to SNAP and also aims to dramatically shift the costs of the program to states. Since then, SNAP enrollment has fallen faster nationally than the government anticipated, with states reducing caseloads as they look ahead to growing cost burdens, said Ty Jones Cox, vice president of food assistance at the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, a Washington, D.C.-based policy institute.</p><p>“SNAP is in the middle of the steepest, fastest decline in participation in decades, and it’s not because the need is any lower,” Jones Cox said, noting enrollment had not dropped this quickly since 1997, during earlier reforms to the food assistance program.</p><p>In Illinois, SNAP enrollment had been trending consistently upwards since the early 2000s as a cash assistance program called Temporary Assistance for Needy Families shrank dramatically after welfare reform in 1996. SNAP became one of the main safety-net programs many low-income households depended on, said James Ziliak, the founding director of the University of Kentucky Center for Poverty Research.</p><p>In Chicago, there are growing signs food insecurity this year is trickling down to residents. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/money/2026/07/21/save-a-lot-stores-set-to-close-saturday-after-years-of-turmoil-recent-ceo-death-threatens-city-funded-deal" target="_blank" ><u>Save A Lot discount grocery stores</u></a> cited cuts to SNAP as one reason it is closing stores. On the West Side, one food pantry is seeing an uptick in lines for food, and online food pantry orders are up. Groups that work with people with physical and mental health disabilities are spending long days helping clients get SNAP benefits restored.</p><p>For people like Salinas Torres, the need for food hasn’t gone away. It was her first time at the food pantry hosted by the nonprofit El Hogar Del Niño Child and Family Center, and it was a relief. She had recently taken herself to the hospital after feeling so stressed out about her household’s finances.</p><p>“I feel pressured wondering if we are going to make it today or not,” she said in Spanish. “When they told me about this pantry, I thought it’s a way for me to not worry for at least a week.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Two of Irene Salinas Torres’ children, Antonella, 8, and Tadeo, 3, help workers load the family’s van with boxes of groceries from the El Hogar Del Niño food pantry.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>A contracting safety net </h3><p>It was only a few years ago, during the COVID pandemic, that SNAP benefits were expanded — and people’s idea of how the government should support residents widened, said Carolyn Barnes, an associate professor at the University of Chicago Crown Family School of Social Work, Policy and Practice.</p><p>“In the last five years, the safety net, as low-income families know it has, seesawed,” Barnes said. “It went from being super accessible and generous in an unprecedented fashion, to now being incredibly difficult to access and vulnerable to more cuts.”</p><p>This pattern — expansion followed by contraction — has been happening for decades, Barnes said. One difference now is how quickly SNAP reforms, embedded in H.R. 1, happened compared to welfare reform efforts in the 1990s.</p><p>“A lot of states didn’t know the potential impact of a lot of these [SNAP] administrative changes,” Barnes said. “So a lot of this feels rushed … and less like [a] concerted, planned out 20-year campaign that led up to welfare reform.”</p><p>In 1996, then-President Bill Clinton, a Democrat, signed into law changes to welfare reform that were meant to reduce dependency on government aid and push people into the workforce, according to an analysis from the Brookings Institution, a Washington, D.C., public policy nonprofit.</p><p>But many interpreted the reform as an attack on Black women, Barnes said.</p><p>“The welfare queen rhetoric that [President Ronald] Reagan popularized,” Barnes said, “this was about self-sufficiency, familial responsibility, dads need to be involved in caring for their kids.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-dc0000" name="html-embed-module-dc0000"></a><div style="min-height:537px" id="datawrapper-vis-dVP57"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/dVP57/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-dVP57"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/dVP57/full.png" alt="SNAP enrollment grew over time as welfare rolls shrunk in Illinois (Line chart)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>The reform targeted the welfare program that became TANF. It provides financial assistance for a finite period to pregnant women and families to pay for food, shelter and utilities.</p><p>One year after that reform, TANF enrollment in Illinois decreased by about 12%, according to data from the University of Kentucky Center for Poverty Research. Over the long-term, the rates fell through the floor.</p><p>Families on TANF had been automatically enrolled in SNAP before welfare reform, but that changed after 1996. In places like Illinois, that led to a drop in food assistance enrollment, from 1.1 million people in 1995 to 760,472 people five years later, according to center data.</p><p>That could be caused in part by families on TANF leaving both programs, Ziliak said. In the years after, only about half of those eligible for food assistance were enrolled, he said, so there was a push to get people signed up. From 2004 to 2024, there were always more than 1 million people receiving food assistance in Illinois, with spikes to 2 million in 2013 and in 2023.</p><p>Meanwhile, TANF numbers continued to plummet. By 2024 — three decades after welfare reform — there were only 20,022 Illinois residents enrolled. Participation since the Clinton era decreased by 96%.</p><p>“What we do know is that, from what we can pick up from surveys, is that their overall family incomes fell after welfare reform,” Ziliak said.</p><h3>States face costly financial burden </h3><p>In this first year of SNAP reform, the state of Illinois has tried to keep as many people on the food assistance program as possible, in contrast to other states that have scrambled to comply by making it more difficult for households to stay eligible.</p><p>But embedded in H.R. 1 are new cost-sharing requirements for states that will put increasing financial pressure on Illinois and other states.</p><p>To start, Illinois officials estimate one provision amounts to approximately $80 million annually in new administration costs.</p><p>There is also a major penalty looming. Starting in fiscal year 2029, or fall 2028, Illinois could be on the hook for up to $550 million annually in new costs, based on current enrollment, according to an <a class="Link" href="https://civicfed.org/blog/illinois-fails-lower-snap-payment-error-rates-targeted-hr-1" target="_blank" ><u>analysis by the Civic Federation</u></a>. Illinois, along with advocates and other states subject to this penalty, are pushing for those penalties to be delayed to 2030.</p><p>The penalty is for a so-called SNAP “error rate” that is considered high. That rate is calculated off a small sampling of cases and is used to measure benefit overpayment or underpayment, according to the Illinois Department of Human Services. The measurement has existed for decades but has never before been used to shift costs to states. The Trump administration says it’s using it to push for greater accuracy and efficiency.</p><p>States with a rate above 6% will have to pay for a portion of SNAP benefits. Illinois’ most recent rate was nearly 15%, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture. State officials shared efforts to drive that percentage down, including tech improvements and adding caseworkers, but in a statement it dismissed the Trump administration’s stated goals, calling this a "penalty scheme" that is being used to "squeeze billions of dollars from state taxpayers."</p><p>The pressure to reduce the error rate appears to be driving some of the drastic changes in enrollment in places like Arizona, where officials are requiring more documentation to get food assistance, <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/20/us/politics/snap-food-stamps-arizona.html?unlocked_article_code=1.zlA.8Wwh.DvlJy4sEAVoD&smid=url-share" target="_blank" ><u> The New York Times</u></a> reported.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-930000" name="image-930000"></a> <picture entries.summary: <p>The first and last time the Chicago City Council passed a sweeping renters’ rights ordinance was in 1986.</p><p>Ronald Reagan was president, Stevie Wonder and Lionel Richie were atop the Billboard 100 chart, and the median rent <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/interactive/chicago-rents-climbing-fast-housing-crisis/chicago-rent-time-machine/" target="_blank" ><u>in some Chicago neighborhoods was around $515</u></a>.</p><p>Forty years later, tenants face sky-high rents, bidding wars and piles of fees. They struggle to track down their own landlords when problems arise in their buildings. Landlords themselves face rising costs and property taxes that can make it hard to keep rent affordable.</p><p>Many agree the city’s Residential Landlord and Tenant Ordinance (RLTO) is due for a renovation.</p><p>Mayor Brandon Johnson has pitched a plan backed and crafted by tenants rights groups and housing advocates. A group of City Council members have pitched an alternative, more landlord-friendly version.</p><p>Both sides agree the bulk, or “98%,” of their proposals are the same. But the 2% where they diverge mark key differences.</p><p>In Chicago, there are more than 600,000 renters — more than half of all households in the city and an undeniably significant bloc of voters. Housing affordability could factor into the city's upcoming mayoral and City Council elections. And as those races begin gearing up this fall, the debate over City Hall’s competing rental ordinances could come to a head.</p><p>Here’s what you need to know.</p><h3><b>Who’s behind each proposal and what are the politics here?</b></h3><p>Tenants rights groups have for years sought an overhaul of the city’s existing rental laws, seeking both modern-day protections and a second chance to fight for components left out of the original ordinance.</p><p>They finally found a City Hall ally in Johnson, who campaigned on the idea “housing is a human right” and introduced the <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/housing/2026/05/29/mayor-brandon-johnson-ordinance-protects-chicago-renters-housing?subscription=true" target="_blank" ><u>“Protecting Renters Ordinance,”</u></a> or PRO, in June. He called it the culmination of “years and years and years of struggle.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a increasingly frayed, and a month later, moderate and conservative alders were out with their own version, dubbed the “Fair and Accountable Illinois Rental Ordinance,” or FAIR.</p><p>So far, the group is made up of 23 out of roughly 30 alders who opposed Johnson’s failed pitch for a new tax on corporations. Spearheaded by Ald. Gilbert Villegas (36th), the group also sought help from a political action committee called One Future Illinois, made up of wealthy and influential business people.</p><p>No tenants rights groups were consulted before the ordinance was introduced.</p><p>The Neighborhood Building Owners Association, which represents small and mid-sized landlords, was measured in its reaction to the FAIR ordinance, saying in a statement there are “still important issues to resolve” in order to “refine the ordinance.”</p><h3><b>Who is considered a small landlord?</b></h3><p>Currently, property owners who live in their building with six or fewer units are considered small landlords, and that building is exempt from most of the city’s renter laws — a definition maintained in the proposal from the mayor.</p><p></p><p>FAIR, the proposal from City Council, would create three tiers of landlords. Small landlords could own up to 12 rental units throughout Chicago and need not live in any of the buildings.</p><p>Villegas said the intent is to help “mom-and-pop” landlords expand their portfolios.</p><p>“The approach there was to help try to help those folks that are in this housing-providing business the opportunity to grow a little bit, and differentiate between [corporations like] Blackstone and J.P. Morgan versus Mr. and Mrs. Morgan, who live on the block,” Villegas said.</p><p>But some housing advocates say expanding exemptions to buildings with up to 12 units that are not owner-occupied could result in thousands of Chicago renters losing long-held tenant protections.</p><p>“FAIR is worse for tenants than the status quo and cannot be reasonably considered to be a tenant protection retaliation against tenants who report code violations.”</p><p>Hertz also said given the prevalence of <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/housing/2025/09/05/chicago-landlords-renters-property-management-llc?subscription=true" target="_blank" ><u>limited liability companies</u></a> as a form of property ownership, it would be difficult to verify “who fits in that [small landlord] category and who doesn’t.”</p><h3><b>The long-awaited rental registry</b></h3><p>To help track ownership and enforce city code, tenant groups have long advocated for a citywide rental registry, which would require landlords to disclose key information about their properties. <a class="Link" href="https://www.localhousingsolutions.org/housing-policy-library/rental-registries/" target="_blank" ><u>Dozens of cities</u></a> across the country already have versions of such a database.</p><p>Both PRO and FAIR call for a rental registry, but each proposal takes a significantly different approach.</p><p>FAIR would require that landlords provide only the property address and contact information for “the owner or the owner’s authorized agent” and for the person in charge of tenants’ repair requests.</p><p>PRO would require additional information, including details on who is responsible for an LLC or trust that owns the property. This, housing advocates say, would allow the city to identify neglectful landlords who may be hiding behind corporate entities.</p><p>“It's really important that the registry be set up to succeed, to make sure that the city is getting out of the registry what it intends to,” Hertz said.</p><p>Villegas said “if there’s further discussions about the content that needs to be collected, we’re open to that.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-110000" name="image-110000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/6c056ba/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5060x2840+0+267/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fdb%2Fd8%2F6aa291d448eea41e3ec63ddef654%2Fcouncil-260521-3.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/1c16221/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5060x2840+0+267/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fdb%2Fd8%2F6aa291d448eea41e3ec63ddef654%2Fcouncil-260521-3.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a632d6d/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5060x2840+0+267/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fdb%2Fd8%2F6aa291d448eea41e3ec63ddef654%2Fcouncil-260521-3.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Ald. Gilbert Villegas (36th) speaks with Anthony Quezada (35th) before a City Council meeting at City Hall July 15.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Jeremy Battle/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>He favors using “off-the-shelf technology” and AI models to manage the registry, instead of the city charging a rental registry fee to maintain a new database.</p><p>Under the mayor’s PRO proposal, a new Bureau of Rental Housing Services would administer the registry and enforce the law. Villegas opposes “more red tape … and more government” and said work should be left up to the Chicago Department of Buildings.</p><p>Housing advocates and the mayor’s team say that agency is already stretched thin and no city department is currently dedicated to enforcing renters’ rights. Tenants typically rely on 311 calls and lawsuits.</p><h3><b>‘Just cause’ could be the hardest fight for tenant rights groups</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Alders behind the FAIR ordinance appear most concerned with the “just cause” provisions in the mayor’s proposal.</p><p>Currently, landlords aren’t required to give a reason when they don’t want to renew a tenants lease, which could be to rehab a property, convert it to condos or demolish it.</p><p>Under the mayor’s proposal, landlords would need to disclose the reason and pay relocation assistance to tenants who aren’t at fault. The relocation payment would range from around $3,000 to $5,000 for most landlords.</p><p>When asked if there was a dollar amount he and other alders could agree to, Villegas said, “If this does pass with a relocation fee, I can tell you that ultimately it's going to end in rents going up.”</p><p>However, tenant advocates say that has not been the case in cities like Los Angeles and San Diego, where — despite enacting just cause provisions — rents <a class="Link" href="https://www.kpbs.org/news/economy/2026/03/27/san-diego-rents-declined-more-than-19-of-nations-top-20-markets-following-surge-in-supply" target="_blank" ><u>decreased</u></a>, and <a class="Link" href="https://www.cbsnews.com/losangeles/news/new-los-angeles-apartment-developments-drive-rental-prices-down-study-finds/" target="_blank" ><u>development</u></a> has continued. <a class="Link" href="https://nlihc.org/tenant-protections" target="_blank" ><u>Dozens of municipalities</u></a> have just cause provisions in place.</p><h3><b>Is a compromise possible? </b></h3><p>There are some signs of potential compromise. Villegas said he has met with the mayor’s office about his proposal, plans to meet tenants rights groups and says revising his ordinance is “just a matter of continuing dialogue.”</p><p>Progressive firebrand Ald. Byron Sigcho-Lopez (25th), who chairs the housing committee, said it’s possible “that we can ease some of the content in the [PRO] ordinance.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-660000" name="html-embed-module-660000"></a><div style="min-height:984px" id="datawrapper-vis-vfJvO"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/vfJvO/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-vfJvO"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/vfJvO/full.png" alt="Key differences in the two renter protection ordinances (Table)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>But the divisiveness seeded during Chicago’s contentious budget season last fall has not waned.</p><p>“If the mayor wants to take the stance that whatever he introduces is the gospel, then we're going to find ourselves in not a good position,” Villegas said.</p><p>Johnson has slammed the opposition bloc in the press, calling their fight against the corporate head tax and, now, against increased renter protections “incredibly disappointing.”</p><p>Advocates hope ia meaningful compromise is still viable in a divisive political moment.</p><p>Regardless of the final proposal’s acronym, “what’s really important,” Hertz said, is “having members of council talk to each other, talk to advocates on all sides, and obviously the administration” to ensure that whatever passes doesn’t place “undue burdens on landlords” while still “advancing the interests of Chicago renters.”</p>
